sessions.conversationStarter: Role-play bumping into each other in a café: greet, apologise, order, thank, and say goodbye, once in each language.
Pick a group photo and point at people: who is he, who is she, which one is us?
Each say three true sentences about your day using today's verbs. The teacher corrects gently.
Take turns asking each other five questions using only today's question words. Answers can be in English.
Play quick-fire: one of you asks yes/no questions and the other answers using only these words.
Plan tomorrow together out loud: what are we doing now, today and tomorrow?
Do this session over a meal: name everything on the table in both languages.
Walk around your home together and name the rooms and things you pass.
Show each other family photos and introduce everyone, using as many of today's words as you can.
Each share one thing you want, one thing you like doing, and how you feel today.
Take turns describing something in the room with today's words. The other one guesses what it is.
Count things around you in both languages, then show each other how you count on your fingers.
Hide something small, then guide the other one to it using only here, there, left and right.
Build the longest sentence you can by chaining and, or, but and because. The sillier the better.
Point at five things and ask how to say each one in the other's language. Who do you both know, and what do you know about them?
Each name three things you can do, one thing you must do this week, and ask permission for something silly.
Describe how you'd get from home to your favourite place in town: which streets, by car or by train?
Tell each other about your work or study day, then about your favourite teacher at school.
Walk through tomorrow by the clock: what happens in the morning, in the evening and at night?
Play shop with things on the table: one sells, one buys, and you haggle over every price.
Swap phone numbers, birthdays and ages using only 1–10, then race each other counting backwards from ten.
Describe people in a photo or on the street: a man, a woman, a girl. Then explain what your names mean.
Point at things around the house and argue playfully about whose they are.
Take turns miming one of today's activities. The other names it in the language they're learning.
Pass things back and forth across the table, saying what you give, take and need.
Each share an opinion starting 'I think…'. The other asks a question about it, and you both check you understood.
Describe today's weather, then the weather where each of you grew up.
Play I-spy with colours: 'I see something red…'
Share something you always do, often do and never do. Then ask: have you already…? Not yet?
Play Simon Says with head, hands and eyes, then talk about the last time you were sick.
Open the wardrobe together and name what you're each wearing today, and what you'd wear to a wedding.
Cook something simple together and name every pot, plate and glass you touch.
Go through the fridge or fruit bowl: name everything, then each pick your favourite and least favourite.
Play restaurant: one of you is the waiter with a made-up menu, the other orders and asks for the bill.
Plan a dream trip together: where do you fly, what goes in the suitcase, how long is the holiday?
Describe where things are in your home: what's upstairs, downstairs, next to the sofa, near or far from the door?
Plan your next visit to friends or family: who do you visit, where do you meet, how long do you stay?
Go through last week day by day: what did you do yesterday, at the weekend, and who got up earliest?
Share your favourite season and month, and what the seasons were like where each of you grew up.
Each tell a story about a film or moment that made you laugh or cry. The other asks how it felt.
Look through photos on your phones together and describe a few. Who did you last call or message?
Rate things from easy to hard: cooking, learning German, learning Chinese, getting up early. Fast or slow?
Explain how to make tea or coffee step by step: first, then, and finally. The other follows the instructions.
Play a hiding game: hide the keys and guide each other with clues about windows, chairs, lights and the sofa.
Talk about pets you've had or would like, and your favourite trees, mountains and animals.
Each name a song, a film and a sport you love. Sing a line or show a dance move if you dare.
Play twenty questions: one thinks of something, the other asks. Answer with 'maybe', 'of course' or 'definitely'.
Talk about the last thing you each bought: which shop, how much did it cost, was it cheap or expensive?
Tell each other a favourite memory of a wedding you've been to, and what you miss when you're apart.
Plan a birthday party for a friend: what do you celebrate with, what present do you give, what do you wish them?
Walk each other through your morning, step by step, from the alarm to the front door.
Taste-test something from the kitchen together: is it sweet, salty, or both?
Describe your ideal breakfast, then compare a German breakfast with a Chinese one.
Draw a quick map of your neighbourhood and mark the supermarket, park, bank and post office.
Plan a trip across your city using only buses, trains and bikes. Who gets there fastest?
Play Simon Says again, this time with legs, arms, mouth, nose and ears.
Role-play a visit to the pharmacy: one is sick, the other is the pharmacist.
Describe three friends or family members using today's words. The other guesses who.
Cook or bake something and argue about the amounts: a little, enough, or more?
Compare two things you each love, like your home towns, and say which is better.
Split this week's chores between you, then name everything that's broken in your home.
Make a plan for next weekend together, and then share one big plan for the future.
Share a favourite childhood memory each. What do you remember, and what have you forgotten?
Each explain a word from your language that has no good translation.
Read out phone numbers, prices and years to each other. The other writes them down.
Show each other photos of a river, lake, sea or forest you love, and describe them.
Make animal sounds in turn; the other names the animal in the language they're learning.
Play a quick game together: cards, rock-paper-scissors or anything with a winner and a loser.
Share one hope, one dream and one wish for the next year.
Practise saying each little phrase at the right moment: welcome each other, raise a glass, say good night.
Draw your family tree for each other and name everyone on it. Who is older, who is younger?
Play bar: one of you orders drinks, the other serves. Then swap languages.
Plan tomorrow's lunch and dinner together. Say when you're hungry, and when you've had enough.
Give each other a tour of your home (or a dream home), naming each room as you walk in.
Hide a small thing in the room. The other looks for it while you both say what you open, close and use.
Give each other commands to act out: walk, run, stand, lie down. Fastest reaction wins.
Pick up five things around you and compare them: which is longer, shorter, heavier, lighter?
Take turns pointing at things in the room. The other names the colour as fast as they can.
Tell each other one thing that made you angry, nervous, bored and happy this week.
Describe your workplace to each other: your boss, a colleague, your meetings and your breaks.
Walk through your day: what do you do in the morning, at noon and in the afternoon, and for how long?
Pick a film or a dish you disagree about. Give your opinion and say whether you agree with the other.
Look out of the window together, by day or by night, and describe everything you can see in the sky.
Play each other a song you love and tell a short story from your childhood.
Choose a new dish or activity to try together this week. Decide who organises what.
Role-play a visit: one of you is the host, the other the guest. Invite, introduce, and be very polite.
Finish each other's sentences: one starts with 'if…' or 'although…', the other completes it.
Interview each other with five questions using today's question words. Answer as fully as you can.
Tell each other what you would say and do in an emergency abroad. Practise calling for help out loud.
Remember a silly argument you had. Replay it in the other's language, and this time make up properly.
Build a little tower of things on the table, then describe it to each other: what is in, on, under, in front of and behind what?
Open a map and show each other where you grew up, which countries you've been to, and which one you'd like to visit next.
Look into the fridge or a cupboard together: what is there some of, what is there none of, and is anything else missing?
Plan a dinner that mixes both kitchens, with one German dish and one Chinese dish. Who cooks the rice, and who makes the soup?
Rate five things from this week, from a film to the weather: bad, not bad or great? Then praise each other's pronunciation.
Each choose three things in the room and say who they are from, who they are for, and whether you could live without them.
Give each other a one-minute massage, naming each body part from face to feet as you go.
Role-play a doctor's visit: one of you has a cough and a cold, the other examines and prescribes. Then compare how a visit works in each country.
Play hairdresser: one says how they'd like their hair cut, the other pretends to cut it. Then admit who is more scared of the dentist.
Tell each other about something you've only done once, something you'd do again, and something you almost did.
Lay the table together twice, once the German way and once the Chinese way, naming every piece as you put it down.
Cook one thing together, with one of you giving the instructions in the language you're learning. Taste as you go.
Raid the kitchen for something spicy, sour, bitter and salty. Taste each one with your eyes closed and name it.
Explain a custom from home: what does one do, and not do, when visiting someone? Then practise greeting each other's parents politely.
Stand back to back, then compare yourselves with family and friends: who is taller, who is stronger? Be kind.
One of you closes their eyes; the other guides them around the room or to the front door using only today's words.
Talk about what you each love spending money on, what you're saving for, and whether you pay by cash, card or phone.
Go through your monthly costs together: rent, electricity, insurance. Compare them with what you'd pay where the other grew up.
Describe your day three times, turning it up each time: a bit tired, quite tired, extremely tired. Who exaggerates better?
Walk through your home and judge every room: bright or dark, loud or quiet, comfortable or not? Pick the best spot.
Plan a real weekend away: where to, which hotel, what is there to see? Look something up and pretend to book it.
Role-play at the airport: your flight is late and someone is waiting to pick you up. Call them and explain.
Plan a night out for this month: cinema, concert, museum or bar? Decide who gets the tickets.
Say the same simple sentence with and without today's little words, and listen to how the mood changes. Then contradict each other for fun.
Tell each other about something surprising that happened this week, step by step. The other keeps asking: and then what happened?
Describe your evening routine: what do you do before dinner, while you cook, and until you fall asleep?
Tell each other the story of your first hug or first kiss as you remember it, and share the pet names your families use.
Each finish these sentences honestly: I'm proud of you because…, I trust you because…, I was a little jealous when…
Ask each other for five small favours as politely as you can. The other only says yes if it was polite enough.
Send each other a message, a photo and an email in the language you're learning, saying out loud what you're doing.
Check each other's phones: how much battery, how much screen time? Then say what annoys you most about your devices.
Find a real form, on paper or online, and help each other fill it in. Then compare the paperwork in both countries.
Describe your most stressful day at work this month. When did you finally get to go home, and how do you switch off?
Make five predictions about next year, from 'definitely' to 'probably'. Add one thing that unfortunately won't happen.
Light a candle or step outside under the sky, and describe a night outdoors you remember: the fire, the air, the stars.
Go for a walk together, phones away, and describe what you see. Then plan a hike: where to, and what goes in the backpack?
Choose three words that are hard to pronounce in each language and coach each other. Then translate a short message together.
Compare your calendars: who is free when this week? Agree on one thing to do together, or let the other one choose.
Describe your family's biggest holiday of the year: what do you eat, who comes, and what do you give each other?
Each share one goal for the coming year, one thing you're excited about, and how the other can help you prepare.
Plan a move together, real or imagined: which flat, who carries what, and what goes in which box? Then dictate your addresses to each other and write them down.
Walk through your home, or a furniture shop online, and name each piece in both languages. Then furnish an empty room together: what goes in the wardrobe, what on the shelf, what in the drawer?
Open the fridge and say what's inside. Then go round the flat: which machine do you use most, and which could you live without? Compare a typical German kitchen with a Chinese one.
Describe the building you live in: which floor, lift or stairs, is there a balcony? Then describe your dream flat while the other one draws it, and check the drawing together.
Sort a pile of laundry together and say what you're doing: what's wet, what's dry, what needs ironing or folding? Then agree who does which laundry job this month.
Lay out what's in your bathroom and name each thing in both languages. Then write a shopping list together: what's running out, and whose shampoo keeps disappearing?
Tell each other how you slept and what you dreamt last night. Then compare: when does your alarm go off, who falls asleep first, and who steals the blanket?
Go through your week from Monday to Saturday: what's fixed on each day? Find the one evening that suits you both and plan something for it.
Describe your perfect lazy Sunday from waking up to going to bed. Which parts are the same for both of you, and where do you have to meet in the middle?
Open your calendars and say today's date in both languages. Then quiz each other: what's the date the day after tomorrow? What happened the day before yesterday? When exactly did you two meet?
Confess: who is usually on time and who runs late? Then plan tomorrow together with exact times, and practise politely moving one appointment to another day.
Write a market list of five fruits and vegetables each and read it out. Then describe one without naming it, by colour, size and taste, and let the other one guess.
Line up the bottles and jars from your kitchen and name them in both languages. Then explain one sauce or dressing from home step by step: what goes in, and how much?
Describe your favourite cake or sweet from childhood: what's in it, and who made it or where did you buy it? Then plan a Kaffee und Kuchen afternoon and decide who brings what.
Look up the forecast for the places where each of you grew up and report it in the other's language, with temperatures. Then tell the story of the worst storm you remember.
Describe exactly what the other one is wearing today, from top to toe. Then choose outfits for three occasions: a job interview, a hike, and dinner with the parents.
Empty your bags or pockets and name everything in both languages. Then play 'leaving the house': one says what to take for rain, sun or cold, and the other checks it's all there.
Role-play a clothes shop: one is the customer, the other the assistant. Ask for a size, try it on, say it's too tight or too loose, and decide whether to buy it or take it back.
Show each other the last thing you ordered online and tell its story: where from, how long it took, was it reduced, would you send it back? Compare how deliveries work in Germany and in China.
Explain how people usually pay where you grew up: cash, card or phone? Then role-play paying in a shop where your first way of paying doesn't work.
Describe a car journey you know well, with every turn, traffic jam and parking space. Then compare learning to drive and the traffic in your two countries.
Explain your daily route by public transport: where do you get on, which line, where do you get off? Then role-play a taxi ride and tell the driver where to stop.
Draw a rough map of each of your countries and mark north, south, east and west. Explain where your family lives and what differs between the regions: food, weather, dialect.
Describe the way from your front door to your favourite café with as many little direction words as you can: across the street, through the park, round the corner, opposite the bank.
Give each other commands around the room and act them out: push the chair, pull the door, lift the box, throw the cushion, don't drop it! Then compare door signs: Drücken or Ziehen, 推 or 拉?
Close your eyes while the other hands you things from the kitchen to smell and touch. Describe what you notice and guess what it is. Then name the smells and sounds of your childhood home.
Collect ten objects and sort them by feel: soft or hard, smooth or slippery, thick or thin, wet or dry. Then describe your ideal bed, towel and winter coat.
Show each other old family photos: who looks like whom? Then play each other three songs or voices and say what they sound like and how they make you feel.
Look at a group photo or at the things on your table and make statements: each of us…, both of them…, some…, several…, this one… The other says whether it's true and puts it right.
Tell the story of how you met, each in the other's language, with plenty of him, her, us and each other. Then name three things you do for each other and one thing each of you does alone.
Plan a weekend trip full of conditions: 'I don't know whether…', 'take a jacket so that…', 'hurry up, otherwise…', 'it's raining, but we're going anyway'. Each of you has to use all five words.
Tell each other about school: your best and worst subject, a teacher you remember, an exam that went wrong. Then set each other three small homework tasks using this week's words.
Interview each other for your dream job: why do you want it, what experience do you have, what salary do you expect? Do it once in each language, then say honestly who would get the job.
Tell each other about one thing you failed at and what you learned from it, and one success you're proud of. Then name something you nearly gave up, and cheer each other on.

Each bring one small real problem: what to cook, what to give a friend, where to go on holiday. The other gives three pieces of advice in the language they're learning; then say which one you'll actually follow.

Tell each other a joke from your country and explain why it's funny, or why it stops being funny once translated. Then pick three topics you never run out of things to say about, and chat about one for five minutes.
Play two truths and a lie: each says three things about themselves in the language they're learning, and the other finds the lie. Then share one harmless secret you've never told.
Tell each other about a moment you were pleasantly surprised, your most embarrassing moment, and a time you felt lonely. The listener reacts in the language they're learning.
Describe each other's character in five words each, with an example for every one: 'you're patient, because…'. Then say which quality you'd like to borrow from the other.
Tell the story of your first date from both sides: who asked whom, where did you go, what did you think? Then explain how dating and 'making it official' work where each of you grew up.
Ask your families what you were like as babies and tell each other the stories. Then compare how small children are looked after in Germany and in China: who helps, and when does kindergarten start?
Draw both family trees side by side and explain every relative: who is whose daughter, aunt or cousin? Then practise how you would address each of the other's relatives.
Tell your life story in two minutes: where and when you were born, where you grew up, the biggest turn so far. Then talk about someone in your family who has died and what you remember of them.
Each name three things you miss from home and three habits of the other's culture that surprised you. Then cook, play or show each other one piece of 'home' this week.
Talk about the pets you had, wanted, or were never allowed to have. Then decide together: if you got a pet, which one, what would you call it, and who would feed it and take it out?
Play each other one song that means a lot to you and explain why. Which instruments can you hear? Then sing one line of it together in the original language.
Tell each other which sports you played as a child and which you only watch. Then make a realistic exercise plan for next week that you could do together.
Tell each other about your worst fall, cut or accident: what happened, and who helped? Then practise calling an ambulance in the other's language: where you are, what happened, who is hurt.
Sit at one computer and guide each other through a small task in the other's language: open a file, save it under a new name, delete a line, print a page. No pointing allowed!
Show each other the last video or post that made you laugh and explain it in the other's language. Then compare your apps: what do WhatsApp and WeChat each do, and which family groups are you in?

Introduce yourselves as if you were meeting each other's parents for the first time: first name, surname, and what your friends call you. Then tell each other your childhood nicknames and who gave them to you.

Go through the first five months of the year together: whose birthday falls when, what the weather is like in each of your home towns, and what you did this year. Say every date out loud in the other's language.

Plan a summer and an autumn together, month by month from June to October: holidays, festivals, visits home. Then explain one festival from your country that falls in these months and what people eat for it.

Tell each other how the year ends where you grew up: what happens in November and December, and which season you love most? Then put your important dates in one calendar: anniversaries, and any birthdays kept by the lunar calendar.

Describe a normal week to each other without using 'always' or 'never': what you usually do, sometimes do, and hardly ever do. Then guess each other's habits: 'You rarely…', 'You usually…'. Who knows whom better?

Trade numbers that matter: your ages, your parents' ages, the population of your home towns, a monthly rent, the price of a flight. Write each one down as the other says it and check. Chinese counts in ten-thousands, so take your time!

Each bring one small real problem from this week (a broken thing, a full calendar, a misunderstanding). Explain what happened and why, then work out a solution together in the other's language. End with: 'It'll work out!'

Tell each other about a time you got something completely wrong: you mixed up two words, two people or two days. When did you notice? Then test each other on pairs of words that are easy to confuse in each language.
Compare the rules you grew up with: what did your parents allow and forbid, and at what age? Then write three house rules for your own home, each of you in the other's language, and negotiate them.
Rearrange a corner of your home together. One of you gives the orders in the other's language (put this there, hang that here, fetch the box), the other carries them out and says what they are doing.

Play hide-and-seek with a small object. The seeker asks questions in the other's language (Is it somewhere in the kitchen? Inside something? Outside?) and complains: 'I've looked everywhere!' Then swap.

Tell each other about school and student days: your best and worst teacher, what you studied (or wanted to) and what student life was like. Then grade each other as language teachers this year, with reasons!

Describe your day with as many place and reason words as you can: who you were with, where you waited, what you did instead of something else, and what went wrong because of what. Your partner counts the little words.

Each of you names three things you love doing, three you can't stand and one you simply don't care about. The other has to guess the reasons. Then find one new hobby you'd both be willing to try together.
Each pick one piece of news from this week, from your own country, and explain it simply in the other's language: where, who, what happened? Then tell each other what you wish for the world.

Open session one and flip through your first words together. Tell each other the first sentence you remember saying, the word that took you longest, and three things you can do now that you couldn't at the start.

Thank each other properly, in the other's language, for three specific things from this year of teaching: a correction, a patient explanation, a laugh. Then pay each other two compliments and practise accepting them.
Each secretly prepare a tiny surprise for the other: a note, a snack, a song. Present it with a short toast in the other's language, look each other in the eye, and clink glasses.

Imagine yourselves at eighty. Where is your home, who cooks, which language do you argue in, and what adventures are behind you? Tell the story to each other in the other's language, then say one thing you promise to keep doing.

sessions.theme: The last lesson & the next step
sessions.conversationStarter: Celebrate: you have taught each other a thousand words! Each give a little speech in the other's language: your favourite word, your funniest mistake, and what made this year unforgettable. Then agree on your next step together: a trip, a film without subtitles, a phone call with the family.
